yes_case.case: The closest historical episodes are the original 1996 Ganga Water Treaty negotiation and the 2015 Land Boundary Agreement ratification. This episode differs fundamentally from 1996 because the baseline political architecture is no longer built on mutual suspicion of water-withholding infrastructure like the Farakka Barrage, but on deeply integrated grid connections, multimodal transit, and comprehensive security interdependency that render water sharing a technical component of a broader, unbreakable strategic partnership. It differs from 2015 because while that agreement resolved long-standing enclaves through sudden high-level political will bypassing bureaucratic inertia, the current Ganga renewal is insulated by institutionalized river-basin frameworks and joint scientific committees that have already established baseline data parity, removing the primary historical friction point of upstream-downstream distrust.
key_evidence: The 1996 Ganga Water Treaty established a 30-year sharing formula based on specific 10-day water flow averages at Farakka.

The 2015 Land Boundary Agreement demonstrated that both New Delhi and Dhaka possess the capacity to execute landmark bilateral treaties at the highest executive levels regardless of domestic political friction.
Bilateral connectivity frameworks in power, transit, and security built over the last decade have created a high-stakes cooperative equilibrium absent during the 1996 negotiations.

no_case.case: The closest historical episodes are the initial 1996 Ganga Water Treaty negotiations under Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda and Sheikh Hasina, and the stalled 2011 Teesta River water-sharing agreement negotiations under Prime Minister Manmohan Singh and Sheikh Hasina. This episode differs from the 1996 success because the political landscape in Bangladesh has fundamentally shifted post-August 2024 with the interim government under Muhammad Yunus, replacing a historically cooperative Awami League regime with one exhibiting strained diplomatic ties with New Delhi. Furthermore, it differs from the 2011 Teesta failure—where domestic federal pushback from West Bengal Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee derailed the pact—because the current Ganga renewal faces both domestic Indian basin-state reallocation demands and a newly assertive, nationalist Bangladeshi administration less inclined to accept status-quo asymmetry. The presence of acute domestic political transitions in both capitals makes a binding successor agreement distinctively more contentious than the stable bureaucratic alignment that pushed the 1996 treaty across the finish line.
key_evidence: The 1996 Ganga Water Treaty was signed under conditions of strong bilateral political alignment between the Awami League and United Front governments, which is absent following the ouster of Sheikh Hasina in 2024.
The 2011 Teesta water agreement collapsed due to sub-national vetoes from West Bengal, mirroring current complications regarding upstream Indian infrastructure demands on the Ganga basin.
The current interim administration in Dhaka has signaled a pivot in bilateral foreign policy priorities away from the uncritical water-sharing concessions characteristic of the prior decade.
no_case.strength_reason: The structural absence of the unique historical political alignment that enabled the 1996 treaty, combined with heightened nationalist sensitivities in post-2024 Dhaka mirroring the 2011 Teesta deadlock, creates a near-insurmountable analogical barrier to signing a successor accord.
